Mongolia adopted the Cyrillic alphabet for Mongolian in 1941, under strong Soviet influence, and it came into general use from 1946. It replaced the classical vertical Mongolian script, which goes back to the Uyghur script taken up under Genghis Khan.

The Mongolian version uses the Russian letters plus two extra vowels, Ө and Ү. It follows the spoken Khalkha dialect closely, where the old script kept a much older spelling, so it was easier to learn, and with Soviet-style schooling literacy rose fast. A Latin alphabet had been tried briefly in the early 1930s and dropped.

The switch also cut Mongolians off from their own written past and from the Mongols of Inner Mongolia in China, who still use the vertical script. After the 1990 revolution there were plans to bring the old script back. They faded, but it is taught in schools again, and a 2015 law required official documents to be written in both scripts from 2025. Compare Uzbekistan's move to Latin letters and the older Soyombo script.
